questions.question: What is the discrete logarithm problem in a cyclic group ⟨g⟩ of order q?
options: Given g, h in the group, find x with g^x = h — solving for the exponent
Given g, x in the group, compute g^x — straightforward forward exponentiation
Given g, find the order q of the group generated by the element g
Given two elements h₁, h₂, find their product in the group quickly
questions.explanation: DLP: find x = log_g(h) in the cyclic group. Hardness underpins Diffie-Hellman, DSA, ElGamal.

questions.question: Why does DLP in `(Z/pZ)*` for prime p have sub-exponential attacks while DLP on elliptic curves does not?
options: Multiplicative groups (Z/pZ)* embed in the integers, enabling smoothness-based attacks
Elliptic curve groups have prime order, while (Z/pZ)* has order p − 1 with structure
Multiplicative groups support discrete logs only over primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), limiting them
Elliptic curve groups support batch operations, allowing parallel attack vectors faster
questions.explanation: (Z/pZ)* has multiplicative structure inherited from Z. Index calculus exploits smoothness over a prime factor base. Generic EC groups have no such embedding — only generic √q attacks work.

questions.question: How does Index Calculus solve DLP in `(Z/pZ)*`?
options: Collect relations g^k ≡ ∏ pᵢ^eᵢ (mod p) over a small-prime factor base, then linear-algebra-solve
Iterate x ← f(x) and look for cycle collisions like Pollard-rho for DLP
Brute-force every x in [0, p − 1] checking g^x ≡ h (mod p) directly with fast exp
Apply Coppersmith-style lattice reduction to extract the exponent x from h
questions.explanation: Index Calculus: (1) build factor base of small primes; (2) sieve relations g^k ≡ ∏pᵢ^eᵢ; (3) solve for log_g(pᵢ) via linear algebra mod q; (4) compute log_g(h) via one more relation.

questions.question: Asymptotic complexity of Index Calculus for DLP in `(Z/pZ)*`?
options: L_p[1/3, c] = exp((c + o(1))·(ln p)^(1/3)·(ln ln p)^(2/3)) sub-exponential
L_p[1/2, c] = exp((c + o(1))·√(ln p · ln ln p)) sub-exponential complexity
Polynomial in log p, matching the asymptotic of the AKS primality test
Exponential in log p, matching generic group BSGS / rho attack runtimes
questions.explanation: Modern Number-Field-Sieve-style index calculus is L_p[1/3, ...], matching factoring. Earlier function-field-sieve was L[1/2].

questions.question: Why is Index Calculus considered analogous to GNFS for integer factoring?
options: Both build relations over a smooth factor base, then solve a sparse linear system
Both exploit Tonelli-Shanks roots to identify smooth candidates for sieving
Both run in polynomial time conditional on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
Both reduce to elliptic curve point counting via the Hasse-Weil theorem
questions.explanation: Same template: sieve for smooth relations, then F_q-linear-algebra to recover discrete logs (or, for GNFS, mod-2 dependencies for squares). Sub-exponential L[1/3] for the strongest variants.

questions.question: Which DLP-based group resists Index Calculus and hence permits shorter keys?
options: Elliptic curve group E(F_p) — no known sub-exponential attack on general curves
(Z/pZ)* for p prime — has multiplicative structure exploitable by index calculus
Multiplicative group of F_{p^n} for large n — easier via Function Field Sieve
Class group of imaginary quadratic fields — has sub-exponential attacks too
questions.explanation: Generic EC groups admit only √q algorithms (Pollard-rho, BSGS). No L[c] attack. Hence 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA / DH security.

questions.question: Logjam (2015) exploited weakness in DH key exchange. What was the structural cause?
options: Servers used 512-bit primes; one-time Index Calculus precomputation broke all sessions
Servers reused nonces across sessions; Pollard-rho-for-DLP recovered the private key
Servers chose primes p with smooth p − 1, enabling Pollard p−1 to factor and DLP-solve
Servers downgraded ECC to RSA at the TLS layer, breaking forward secrecy
questions.explanation: Logjam: 'export-grade' DH used 512-bit primes. NFS-DL precomputation per prime (~$0.5M, weeks) → minutes per session. Many servers reused the same 512-bit prime, amortizing the cost across millions of victims.

questions.question: How do you defend a DH-based protocol from Logjam-style attacks?
options: Use 2048-bit primes minimum, or switch to ECDH where Index Calculus does not apply
Use 512-bit primes but with a different prime per connection to prevent precomputation
Use composite moduli n = p·q instead of primes to escape the multiplicative structure
Use Carmichael numbers as moduli to break the index calculus relation gathering step
questions.explanation: 2048-bit prime DH places Index Calculus out of reach for foreseeable computation. ECDH (X25519, P-256) is the modern default — sub-exponential attacks don't apply.
